newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka cabinet undergoes "spring cleaning".
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka cabinet undergoes "spring cleaning".

text.p: A major cabinet reshuffle by Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga on Monday was an attempt by the government to put on a new face for the first time in its nearly three years in power, analysts said.

They said the reshuffle, which saw the sacking of a key minister and the induction of eight newcomers to the cabinet, also drilled home the point that Kumaratunga was less tolerant of dissent among members of her seven-party coalition.
"The reshuffle seem to have brought in more sweeping changes than many anticipated," said Sarath Amunugama, a lawmaker with the main opposition United National Party.
"Frankly, it is an attempt by the government to respond to the fact that it could not deliver the goods in three years. Now they are trying to get their house in order," Amunugama told Reuters.

One notable victim of Kumaratunga's reshuffle, the first since her People's Alliance (PA) government took power in 1994, was Srimani Athulathmudali, leader of the PA constituent Democratic United National Lalith Front (DUNLF), who had held the transport, environment and women's affairs portfolios.
Political sources said Athulathmudali was sacked from the cabinet following recent sharp differences between DUNLF and the government over policy.

"It sends the message that the government is less tolerant of dissent within its ranks. It shows that the ruling leadership is willing to take on its detractors even at considerable risk to itself," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
The PA, which has a one-vote majority in Sri Lanka's 225-seat parliament, relies on the support of coalition members such as the DUNLF and other smaller groups to stay in power.
Athulathmudali herself was not available for comment, but her deputy Ravi Karunanayake said the party was being made to pay the price for not blindly towing the government line.

Karunanayake said the DUNLF had been critical of the government for dragging its feet on issues such as the abolition of the executive presidency and the implementation of devolution proposals to end the country's 13-year-old war with Tamil Tiger separatists. The issues featured prominantly in the PA's election manifesto.
"We will continue to stand firm on principles and will take it issue by issue when deciding our future," Karunanayake said without elaborating on what the party's next move would be.
The reshuffle also took away the portfolio of senior cabinet minister Dharmasiri Senanayake.
Kumaratunga gave Senanayake's key media ministry to Mangala Samaraweera, a close confidant, who also kept his previous job as posts and telecommunications minister.
The government was recently embarrassed over its proposed Broadcast Bill, designed to curb private radio and television stations by making it necessary for them to renew their licences each year.
The bill was shot down by the Supreme Court last month after it was challenged by various media organisations as well as the main opposition UNP.

Health Minister Mohammed Fowzie, who analysts say did not often see eye to eye with the powerful Government Medical Officers Association (GMOA), was given Athulathmudali's transport portfolio, but had his health portfolio taken away.
"We hope we will be able to work together with the new minister without much conflict, unlike earlier," said Charith Fonseka, president of the GMOA.
Amunugama said many of the portfolio changes were from areas that had drawn severe public criticism. "If you look at it like that, it is spring cleaning the government has done."
